Reference

Frequently asked questions

Common decisions and expectations when adopting Kite in a Flutter codebase.

Is Kite a runtime framework?

No. Kite is a development-time CLI. It generates ordinary Dart and Flutter source into your project. Your application does not need to call Kite at runtime.

Does Kite own the generated code?

Your team owns it. Kite tracks generated paths and checksums to support safe upgrades, but the files remain normal source that you can edit and review.

Why are generated repository interfaces empty?

Kite cannot know your real business operations. Empty compile-safe contracts create the architecture boundary without inventing methods, endpoint names, or parameters that may be incorrect.

Does Riverpod use code generation?

No. Kite's Riverpod templates use manually declared Provider, NotifierProvider, and AsyncNotifierProvider patterns.

Can one project use Clean Architecture and MVC?

Yes. Architecture can be selected per feature. A complex transactional feature may use clean layers while a small local settings feature uses MVC.

Why do templates have requires?

Reusable foundations should not be copied into every root template. Requirements let Dio reuse API contracts and Riverpod, while components share one sizing foundation.

Can Kite generate more components?

Yes. Add a component registry entry, manifest, template file, supported command value, and tests. See Extending Kite.

Should I use --force?

Only when intentionally replacing existing files with current template output. Prefer --dry-run first and --skip-existing when preserving existing foundations.

How do I update generated foundations?

Use kite upgrade --dry-run to review changes, then kite upgrade. Modified files should be reviewed instead of replaced silently.
